title: A password check that compares against a format string: the magic value is the credential
index_line: T-0050 · AUTH_DECISION · the stored credential is a constant template, so the string that matches it is a shared secret · c · corroborated
invariant_violated: A credential is assumed to be something only the legitimate user knows, so the comparison is a formality: any value that matches is fine. But if the value it matches is a *constant in the firmware* — and one shaped like a printf template — then the credential is published with the product, and the comparison is all that stands between anyone and the account.

mechanism.does: an attacker presents a username and the constant the firmware compares against, on the management interface
the authentication path reads its expected value from a fixed location rather than from a per-device secret
the comparison succeeds for anyone who supplies the constant
the session is granted full administrative rights with no device-specific material involved
the attacker configures the device — including its VPN policy, which is what made this one notable

sink.auth.jwt-verify.value: the credential-comparison call site — the guard is what is compared against, so the defect is in its right-hand side

source.protocol.value: the management protocol's login exchange (SSH, HTTPS admin, console) — no web exploitation needed

guard.none.value: no per-device secret, no password file, no hashing: the comparison is against a literal

encoding.string.value: the literal itself, including its printf-shaped punctuation, which makes it searchable in a firmware dump

preconditions.expr: the credential comparison uses a constant rather than a stored hash
the management interface is reachable and accepts password authentication
the literal is present in the shipped image (searchable in a dump, not secret)

check.spec: strings firmware.bin | grep -F "<<< %s(un='%s') = %u" || strings firmware.bin | grep -c 'un='

success: a login succeeds with a password that appears verbatim in the vendor's own binary
the credential works on every device of that firmware generation — it is not tied to the device
no failure counter or lockout responds, because nothing about the attempt is anomalous to the code
failure_like: the expected value is derived per device (a hash of a serial, a stored secret)
the interface has been patched to remove the constant
false_positive: a default password that is documented and changeable — that is a hardening problem, not this
a string in the binary that looks like a credential but is never compared against a supplied value

hazards: the highest-value search in any firmware assessment is `strings | grep '%'` — a credential shaped like a format template is a constant comparison
this class is found by diffing a pre-backdoor and post-backdoor build, not by reading source: the code looks like ordinary auth
a constant credential makes every affected device one population, so remediation is a recall-shaped problem, not a patch
the same audit question applies to every 'vendor service account' — who derives its secret, and from what?
non_transfers: systems where the vendor account's secret is generated at manufacture

evidence.target: Juniper ScreenOS 6.2.0r15–6.3.0r19 (CVE-2015-7755), backdoor removed in later builds
